chatam_sofer.en: In Magen Avraham, Maggid Mishneh 20 — note: Here is the rule for this calculation: if you reckon twelve hours from amud hashachar until tzeis hakochavim, and in them forty milin, for everyone it comes out to eighteen minutes per mil; but the Rambam calculates twelve hours from sunrise until sunset alone; and if you hold from amud hashachar until sunrise five milin, and likewise from sunset until tzeis hakochavim, it turns out that from sunrise until sunset there are only thirty milin, and in them twelve hours there will be twenty-four minutes per mil — and this is as Tosafos Yom Tov wrote in his name in chapter 3 of Pesachim. But the truth is that the Rambam holds, as is said, from amud hashachar until sunrise four milin, and likewise from sunset until tzeis hakochavim, and what remains from sunrise until sunset is thirty-two milin, and in them twelve hours it comes out to twenty-two and a half minutes per mil, and this is the main [view]. And so ruled Chek Yaakov siman 459. And what the Rambam wrote regarding prayer, from amud hashachar until sunrise is an hour and a fifth — it should be explained according to what Tosafos wrote in Pesachim 94a s.v. R' Yehuda, that although the beginning of sunset is four milin, nevertheless the last three-quarters of a mil, when the sun has already entered within the thickness of the sky, is called bein hashmoshes; and see also the language of Tosafos in Bava Metzia there; and if so, the same applies at amud hashachar — the first three-quarters of a mil, when the sun begins to emerge, are not fit for prayer at all; and three-quarters of a mil are close to eighteen minutes; when you remove this from four milin, an hour and a fifth remains in approximation. Also the Rambam in chapter 3 of Pesachim holds to say that there, in the Gemara Resh Lakish gave the amoraim the measure of chimutz like from the tower of Ninus to Tiberias, which is a mil; and behold the tower of Ninus and Tiberias — see in the Ran, and it is possible to estimate them; and now, if you would think that that measure is a small mil of twenty-two and a half minutes, then Ulla and Rava in Pesachim 94 would disagree with Resh Lakish, for per them a mil is twenty-four minutes — and for such a thing the Gemara should have said and they disagree with Resh Lakish; rather, perforce from Ninus to Tiberias is also twenty-four minutes, and Resh Lakish calls it a mil. See also the tanna in the beginning of and darkness in the chapter of one who was tamei. And now, although regarding a mil we do not rule like him, nevertheless regarding the measure of chimutz they do not disagree, for it is like from the tower of Ninus, which is twenty-four minutes, which is two-fifths of an hour — see there well and understand carefully. However, I have now found in an ancient book called Kaptor Vaferach, which the author of Tosafos Yom Tov cites well at the beginning of chapter 7 of Sheviis, in Beit Yosef Orach Chayyim at the end of siman 10, and in that book chapter 11 section 68 page 2 s.v. we shall return to Jerusalem, etc., he wrote from Jerusalem to Azazel is like three hours, etc. And behold the rabbi, may his memory be blessed, saw and knew and measured with great precision, and it is one hundred eighty minutes, and in them ten milin for R' Yehuda and R' Yosi in Yoma 67b — if so, perforce a mil is no more than eighteen minutes, and not like the Rambam; and experience and reason will not be denied; and perhaps one may say, a land of deer is written regarding it — so too must be said in what is written there siman 72, the width of the land of Israel is only, etc.; and likewise a land of deer is written regarding it.

chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 1 — the time of prayer, etc. NB — Behold it is explained in the books that one should give charity before every prayer, as it is written, 'and I in righteousness will behold Your face'; and I will explain the reason more, with the Omnipresent's help: behold I saw in Sefer Kav HaYashar from a certain kabbalist that tekhelet in gematria is titain, and therefore it is fitting to look with both eyes at the tzitzis, for 'eye' with 'eye' together with tzitzis adds up thus, and it is as if one fulfilled tekhelet thereby; and in my opinion it appears to correct this with charity, for [it appears it should say tekhelet] which is like the gematria titain — that is, one gives charity and considers it as if he fulfilled tekhelet; and therefore before putting on the tzitzis it is fitting to give charity; and therefore in Midrash on parashas Tetzaveh on the verse 'and it shall be righteousness for you before the the Omnipresent your the Omnipresent' — charity ascends to the throne of glory; and this is since tekhelet resembles the sea, and the sea to the firmament, and the firmament to the throne of glory — if so, through tekhelet one is reminded of the glory of the Glory, and charity is in gematria tekhelet — if so, charity is in place of tekhelet; therefore it too ascends to the throne of glory; and therefore it says, 'and I in righteousness will behold Your face,' like with tekhelet — and it comes out well; understand carefully. May the Omnipresent show us wonders in His Torah, amen. [And see in my composition on Megillas Esther from the year 5633, in explanation of the article Shoshanas Yaakov, what I wrote per the above there, with the Omnipresent's help, and understand carefully.]

turei_zahav.en: And after midnight, etc. In the Tur it is written: if one transgressed and prayed after four hours until midnight, although he does not have reward as prayer in its time, he nevertheless has reward of prayer. Beit Yosef wrote on this two paths. One is that the Tur learned from what the Gemara challenges on Rabanan who say until midnight and no more — and we say: one who erred and did not pray Shacharit prays two Minchah, and it answers: all day he prays and goes until midnight — from here they give him reward of prayer in its time, from here they do not give him reward of prayer, from here they give him reward of prayer in its time they do not give him — from this we learn for R' Yehuda that after four hours it is so: what difference to me after Shacharit for R' Yehuda and what difference after midnight for Rabanan. And he wrote that according to his explanation it is not precise that after Shacharit for R' Yehuda only; rather also until night it would be so, since once the time has passed it would be for R' Yehuda after his time as for Rabanan after their time. And that the Tur only took until midnight is not precise. And he challenged this: since we learn after Shacharit from “one who did not pray Shacharit prays two at Mincha,” let us also learn this matter — that just as when he did not pray Shacharit he has compensation at Mincha, this is specifically when he did not cancel intentionally, but when he cancelled intentionally he has no compensation at all; if so, also for the morning prayer after Shacharit the law would be thus. And why did the Tur write that even if he transgressed intentionally and did not pray before Shacharit, he prays afterward? Therefore he wrote a second path: the Tur learns after Shacharit for R' Yehuda from reasoning — since for Rabanan even lechatchilah he prays until midnight and has reward of prayer in its time, so too for R' Yehuda at least regarding reward of prayer not in its time. And therefore immediately after midnight it is forbidden to pray and it is a blessing in vain. And some say: after Mincha when he prays two — for there he prays in the time of the Mincha prayer. And he brought proof from the words of the Rashba that we will mention shortly; and accordingly Rama wrote his words here that after midnight it is forbidden, etc. And it is difficult on the second path, for we say in the Gemara’s explanation “all day he prays and goes” — implying until night he prays, only he does not have reward like in its time; and this would also be for R' Yehuda, for the challenge is to R' Yehuda like to Rabanan from “one who did not pray Shacharit,” etc.; automatically the answer would also be for him like for Rabanan. And one could ask: why does the Gemara challenge “and all agree until midnight and no more” from “one who did not pray Shacharit” — perhaps it is so that until midnight and no more, but at Mincha it is better since it is the time of prayer? And it seems to me that the first path is true, only that the source of this law is not from “one who did not pray Shacharit,” etc., as Beit Yosef thought; and from this it followed for him to say that if one cancelled intentionally before Shacharit, afterward he has no remedy — and a difficulty emerged for him on the Tur, as stated. Rather the source is from what is stated in the Gemara “all day he prays,” etc.; and this would also be for R' Yehuda. And in the Gemara they said to Rabanan: until midnight he has reward of its time, and afterward all day, even after Mincha, he has reward not in its time. From this we also learn for R' Yehuda that all day he has compensation — only that if it is after Shacharit when the hour of Mincha has not yet arrived, he certainly may pray even lechatchilah, even if he cancelled intentionally until that hour, as stated in the Gemara “all day is time for prayer,” only he does not have reward of prayer in its time. And after the time of Mincha has arrived, which is six and a half hours, then it is forbidden for him to pray at that hour Shacharit, since the time of Mincha has arrived; therefore he must give precedence to the Mincha prayer and afterward pray to complete Shacharit, and he has reward of prayer not in its time. And since in this there is a prohibition to pray before he prays Mincha, therefore they said in this that if he cancelled intentionally until that hour he has no compensation — for after midnight R' Yehuda and Rabanan are equal, that he prays until six and a half, which is half an hour after midnight. And therefore Rif and Rosh did not mention the measure here but stated simply: if he transgressed and prayed after four hours. But Rambam and Tur wrote after four hours until midnight; and they too did not come to exclude that half hour but to exclude after the time of great Mincha. And that they did not write until six hours — because I would have said “until” includes it and he could pray even if six and a half hours had arrived; and in truth it is forbidden until he prays Mincha first — therefore they wrote until midnight, so that even if you say “until” includes it there is no error here, for there remains another half hour. Rather between after Shacharit and until midnight they disagree, and R' Yehuda holds that also in that hour they do not give him reward of prayer in its time, even though he prays immediately at that hour without giving precedence to the Mincha prayer before it. And what Beit Yosef brought as proof for the second path from the responsum of the Rashba — with apology to our master Beit Yosef — it seems to me there is no proof from there, for thus he wrote on that which the conclusion is “one who erred and did not pray Mincha prays two Maariv,” etc.; however specifically in the time of prayer, while he is engaged in his prayer, he returns and completes what he erred in his prayer — but not outside the time of prayer. For if not, what is “prays two Maariv” and “prays two Mincha” that it says? Let it say: one who erred and did not pray Shacharit before midnight returns and prays after midnight; one who erred and did not pray Mincha returns and completes all night, end quote. Our master Beit Yosef thought the Rashba comes to exclude even before the time of Mincha, which is six and a half, that he should not pray. And it does not seem so to me, for the Rashba took the parallel of “one who did not pray Mincha” in his proof — he should have taken “one who erred and did not pray Mincha returns and completes all night,” and there he does not exclude except after the time of the evening prayer, for there is no time interrupting between the end of the time of Mincha and the beginning of Maariv. Rather it is simple that also regarding the morning prayer the Rashba did not come to exclude except that immediately after he prays Mincha he prays to complete Shacharit — and this is explicit in his wording that he wrote “while he is engaged in his prayer,” etc.; but if he waits afterward, compensation does not apply to what he will pray a second time afterward, for otherwise the author of the Talmud would not have tied compensation of Shacharit to the Mincha prayer but would have said that after midnight Rabanan may complete the morning prayer, and similarly for the Mincha prayer all night. Or he intended that compensation be at the time he is engaged in prayer in any case and not afterward. kaf_hachayim.en: (3) There — if he prayed from when the time of dawn arrived, etc. Peri Chadash wrote in note 1, and these are his words: the author was silent here and did not explain; and the main point is that there are three times for the beginning of the time of prayer — and behold, the main fulfillment of its mitzvah is from sunrise, as the early pious ones, for it is written "they shall fear You with the sun"; and for the outset one may pray from when the column of dawn rose and the face of the east brightened, as was the practice; nevertheless if he prayed from when the column of dawn rose he has fulfilled, as we learned in Megillah — and all who acted from when the column of dawn rose have fulfilled; and also the tamid — if they slaughtered from when the column of dawn rose it is not invalidated; but for the outset, all matters whose mitzvah is by day — their main time is from sunrise; except that in the tamid, since all sacrifices must be offered before the afternoon tamid, they advanced the time slightly before sunrise; but if one acted from alos hashachar, it is obvious he has fulfilled — and not as implied from the words of Rabbeinu Yeruham that the Beit Yosef brought and from the words of the author — and this is obvious — end quote. And the Taz, note 1, wrote that the time of dawn-rise is the time before one can see his friend at a distance of four amot; but from the time one can see his friend one may pray for the outset — only the mitzvah from the preferred way is that it is better to pray immediately after sunrise — end quote. And similarly Maamar, note 1, in the name of Rabbeinu Yeruham, and wrote: according to this understanding of Rabbeinu Yeruham's words one should not object so much to those who advance on the days of Selichos, for they do not advance so much as to pray before the time one can recognize his friend — end quote. It follows that for all opinions the mitzvah from the preferred way requires sunrise; and after the fact, if he prayed from alos hashachar even if the face of the east did not brighten he has fulfilled — and so too Magen Avraham, note 3; and so too Eliyah Rabbah, note 1, in the name of the Ramban in Milchamos, first chapter of Berachos, and wrote: and not like Eliyah Rabbah; and Matteh Yehuda, note 1, who wrote that even after the fact he does not fulfill unless the face of the east brightened — see there; and so too is implied from the words of the poskim that from alos hashachar he fulfills. And from when the face of the east brightened — Peri Chadash holds one may pray for the outset; but Maran holds even this is only after the fact, as explained in Shulchan Aruch; and the Taz holds from when one sees his friend at a distance of four amot one may pray for the outset — and so too Rabbeinu Yeruham, as Maamar wrote; but we have not seen Maran divide on this — see above in Beit Yosef. However see what I wrote in siman 25, note 27, that per the secret of the matter one must don tzitzit and tefillin before Keriat Shema of the sacrifices section, and at least before the portion of the tamid — see there; and the time of laying tefillin is from when one sees his friend, as explained in siman 30, seif 1, and in our words at length on that topic. If so, when one waits until the time of laying tefillin and dons tzitzit and tefillin and begins to pray from the Binding of Isaac section onward, with calmness and settled mind, word by word as fitting so that no letter be missing — and in particular the intent of the Divine Names — his Shacharit prayer will be close to sunrise, which is the emergence of the body of the sun upon the earth, as explained in our words above in siman 58, note 10; and fortunate is one who serves his Master properly and is not particular about a short time for prayer, for they are matters that stand at the height of the world.
